approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Y-shaped larch at the base of the Southwest Rib, then three pitches up before this route starts
approach_variants.notes:
Same start as the Southwest Rib: Blue Lake Trailhead, Blue Lake Trail about 1.25 miles to the northwest clearing, then the climber's path up into the basin.

Three pitches at 5.10b as counted here, but understand what the route is: it is pitch 5 of a combined line, about 100 ft of sustained climbing under and through a pair of roofs.
hazards: No ground start; three pitches of another route must be climbed first
A loose block right at the start of the roof pitch
Rappelling back through an overhanging roof is awkward and undocumented, so bailing here means natural gear anchors
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route has no ground start, and that is the most important fact about finding it. You reach it by climbing the first three pitches of the southwest rib, or alternatively by the Northwest Face Boving-Pollock line, and then going left at a ledge where the two roofs come into view.

So the base of the day is the base of the southwest rib, and that has a landmark you can stand under: the Y-shaped larch tree at the base of the southwest rib, left of the southwest couloir. A larch with a forked trunk, at the foot of a rib, with a couloir to its right. That is the aiming point from the basin.

The in-route test is visual and binary: go left at the ledge where the two roofs come into view. Two roofs, stacked. If you can see only one overhang, or none, you have not reached the ledge. If you have climbed more than three pitches of the rib you have gone past it.

A hazard right at the start of the pitch, recorded because it is exactly where a party is committing: there is a loose block right at the start of the roof pitch.

What nobody does here, which answers the obvious question: parties do not reverse this pitch. Rappelling back through an overhanging roof is awkward and is not the documented practice. Most continue up the remaining Southwest Rib pitches to the true summit and take the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete to the rabbit ears then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted anchors down the gully.

rappel_detail.pull: Built for a single 60 m rope, and the stations were placed to give steep, clean pulls clear of the gully.
rappel_detail.notes: First of three fixed rappel stations equipped in recent years on the South Arete; single 60m rope is sufficient for each rap.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed bolt/chain station, climber's right of the summer gully/chimney
hazards: One party found one of these bolted stations placed on a large block that is not attached to the mountain: counted from the bottom it is the third, which with three stations in place is this top one, above the gully. Inspect the rock the bolts are in, not only the hardware, and back it up if you are not satisfied.
The short 5th-class step above the station is exposed with real fall consequence. Stay roped, and place gear on it rather than soloing down.
rappel_detail.station: Top station of the rappel line North Cascade Mountain Guides installed after the June 2022 rockfall: bolts and chains on a big ledge immediately above the small tree that older parties used to sling. All three new stations sit climber's right of the gully and off the line of ascent — skier's left as you face out on the way down — deliberately taking the descent out of the gully feature the route climbs. You reach it by downclimbing the arete's 3rd/4th-class ground plus one short, exposed 5th-class step.

rappel_detail.pull: Steep and fairly clean on a 60 m rope, provided the strands are kept out of the gully when you throw.
rappel_detail.notes: Continues down the arete; short easy downclimbing sections connect stations.
hazards: The gully immediately beside the line is the loose ground that produced the 2022 rockfall. Keep ropes and feet out of it — that is the whole reason this rappel line was moved.
This is a very popular route and stations back up on summer weekends; anything knocked loose lands on the party waiting below.
rappel_detail.station: Second of the three chain-and-bolt stations, on the ledge just above the chockstone, again set off to the side of the climbing line. Short sections of easy downclimbing link it to the station above, and how much you rappel versus downclimb is a party choice.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel returns to the base of the route.
hazards: Talus and slabs immediately below the last station, with the pull zone directly above anyone still coiling ropes.

The alternative descent some parties take instead — traversing to the Southwest Couloir and walking it out — avoids rope work but is loose and can hold firm snow well into summer, so it is not automatically the safer option without an axe.
rappel_detail.station: Lowest chain station. The rappel from it returns you to the base of the route, where the climbers' trail leads back down through talus and slabs alongside the stream to the Blue Lake Trail.

wa_boving_roofs.rappels: 3 single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope from bolted chain anchors on the South Arete descent, each under 30 m, with easy downclimbing between them
wa_boving_roofs.descent: Continue up remaining Southwest Rib pitches to the summit, then descend the South Arete.
wa_boving_roofs.descent_text: Most parties continue up the remaining Southwest Rib pitches to the true summit after the roofs pitch rather than reversing it (rappelling back through an overhanging roof feature is awkward and not the documented practice). From the summit, take the standard South Arete descent: downclimb the arete to the Rabbit Ears, then 3 single-rope rappels (60m rope) from bolted anchors/chains down the gully to the base, returning to the Blue Lake Trail. If bailing below the roofs, natural gear anchors would be needed since no fixed rappel line down the roof pitch itself was documented.

days.note: Climbs the first three pitches of the Southwest Rib, then breaks left through the classic double roofs (~100 ft of powerful 5.10b jamming). Most parties continue up the remaining Southwest Rib pitches to the summit and descend the South Arete.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Y-shaped larch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, walk the maintained trail roughly a mile and a quarter until it opens into a clearing. Leave it at the small stream — often cairned — and follow climbers' tracks up through the slabs alongside the stream into the basin under the west side of the spires.

The meadows here are fragile and heavily used; stay on the established tracks and off the heather.

From the basin, work up the talus toward the west face of South Early Winters Spire, north of the Southwest Couloir.
hazards: fragile alpine meadow crossed by braided tracks — erosion damage and easy to lose the line
shared descent line with South Arete parties, so expect congestion at rappel stations
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the route is marked by a larch tree that forks into two trunks in a clear Y — it is the single agreed-upon landmark for this climb and people navigate to it by name. In front of the Y-larch an easy ledge runs up and away from the tree; scramble that ledge and belay off a solid tree, and the first proper pitch follows cracks straight up through an awkward bulge, well protected, to a ledge at the foot of the feature climbers call the Wavy Crack. If you start at a lower or higher point on the rib you skip that first 5.8+ pitch and arrive at the Wavy Crack having missed the best of the lower climbing — so hunt for the Y-larch rather than roping up at whatever looks like the toe. The rib you want is the buttress immediately north of (left of, looking in) the Southwest Couloir.

wa_sews_sw_rib.rappels: 3 single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope from bolted chain anchors on the South Arete descent, each under 30 m, with easy downclimbing between them
wa_sews_sw_rib.descent: Reverse to the South Arete and downclimb/rappel back to the base.
wa_sews_sw_rib.descent_text: Descend via the South Arete (the standard descent for the peak): downclimbing 3rd/4th class terrain to the Rabbit Ears, then three single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope from bolted chain anchors back toward the Blue Lake basin. Expect delays at rappel stations on busy weekends since South Arete parties are often descending the same line.

itinerary.cal: North Cascades Highway (SR-20) over Washington Pass usually opens in April or May and closes with heavy snow, typically between mid-November and early December — prime dry-rock season is June-September.

days.note: Hike the Blue Lake trail then cut up to the base of SEWS's southwest face, climb 7 pitches of low-5th to 5.8 rock to the summit, then downclimb part of the South Arete and make 3 rappels from bolted stations back to the base.
